column1: # Security guards, and the edit that removes each one.
# Read by scripts/verify-guards.sh. Tab-separated, four fields:
#   file <TAB> search <TAB> replace <TAB> ctest-target:test-name
# The point is not the list. The point is that a guard here is proven to be
# LOAD-BEARING: remove it and the named test must go red. A test that stays
# green when its guard is gone is measuring something else, and there is no way
# to tell that apart from a passing test by looking at a passing test.
# This exists because that happened. Twice on 2026-08-23 a hand-applied
# neutralisation silently did not match the source -- once because the
# replacement text ignored an if-init-statement -- so nothing was neutralised,
# the test passed, and the guard was recorded as proven when nothing had been
# proven at all. The script refuses a search string that does not appear, which
# is the whole fix: a neutralisation that cannot be applied is a failure, not a
# pass.
# `search` must be a single line and must appear EXACTLY ONCE in the file.
# Not every guard in the codebase is here. These are the ones where being wrong
# means reading somebody else's mail, sending plaintext, or handing a message to
# the wrong account.
# --- the decrypted message must not outlive its account -----------------
app/mail/MailController.h
column2: QString decryptedMessageId() const { return decryptedStillOurs() ? m_decryptedMessageId : QString(); }

column1: # --- a reply for a replaced account is never displayed -------------------
# NOT LISTED, deliberately: the same guard on the DECRYPT path

# Remove it and aReplyForAReplacedAccountIsNeverShown stays green, because the
# read-time guard above already refuses to hand the plaintext out -- the entry
# directly above is what covers that property.
# The apply-time check is still worth having and is not dead: without it the
# plaintext is stored in memory rather than discarded, unreachable through the
# getters but present. No black-box test can see that difference, so it is
